core_obligations: Show that if x = r/f is a nonzerodivisor in S^{-1}R with f in S, then its numerator r is a nonzerodivisor in R, which is what makes the identification of the two rings of fractions possible (proof lines 4817-4820).
Conclude Q(R) is isomorphic to Q(S^{-1}R), and specialise to the multiplicative subset of nonzerodivisors of R to get Q(R) isomorphic to Q(Q(R)) (statement lines 4813-4814).
proof_roadmap: Compare the two rings of fractions by writing an element of S^{-1}R as r/f and checking that nonzerodivisors lift along the condition that S consists of nonzerodivisors (proof lines 4817-4820).
Read the particular case off by taking S to be the set of nonzerodivisors of R, which turns S^{-1}R into Q(R).
difficulty_reason: The lemma states that inverting a multiplicative subset S of R made of nonzerodivisors does not change the total ring of fractions, Q(R) being isomorphic to Q(S^{-1}R), and that consequently Q(R) agrees with Q(Q(R)) (statement lines 4809-4815). The proof isolates the one step that could fail, namely the passage from a nonzerodivisor of S^{-1}R to its numerator: if x = r/f with f in S is a nonzerodivisor, then r must be a nonzerodivisor in R, and this is exactly what the hypothesis on S is for (proof lines 4817-4820). The author leaves the assembly of the two rings of fractions to the reader once that step is in hand. H2.
